title: Galileo Puts the Pope's Words in a Fool's Mouth
text:
Cardinal Maffeo Barberini was an admirer of Galileo Galilei and once wrote a Latin poem in his praise. In 1623 Barberini became Pope Urban VIII. Galileo visited Rome and came away believing he could write about the Copernican idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, as long as he treated it as a hypothesis and gave the opposing view a fair hearing. The Pope asked that the book include one of his own favorite arguments: that God, being all powerful, could produce the same effects in ways human reason cannot discover.

The Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared in 1632. It was written as a conversation among three characters. The defender of the old Earth centered view was named Simplicio, and he came off badly throughout. At the very end of the book, the Pope's argument was given to Simplicio.

Urban VIII's enemies were quick to say he had been mocked, and the Pope felt betrayed. He let the Inquisition take up the case. In 1633 Galileo was tried, forced to abjure, and sentenced to house arrest, which lasted until his death in 1642.
lesson: Never ridicule the person whose support you depend on, even indirectly. A patron who feels mocked can become a far more dangerous opponent than one who simply disagreed.
source: Galileo Galilei, Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632); trial documents in Maurice A. Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair (1989)
caveat: Historians debate how much the Simplicio passage itself, as opposed to Church politics and the Thirty Years War, drove Urban's decision.
